title: Lawyer billable hour targets and utilization on Mac: track, fix and hit them in 2026
metaTitle: Lawyer billable hour targets and utilization on Mac, 2026
description: Missed billable hour targets? See what it costs, why it happens and the free fixes that help you track and improve utilization on a Mac.
targetKeyword: lawyer billable hour targets and utilization
secondaryKeywords: how to track billable time on Mac
intro: A billable hour target is the number of billable hours your firm expects you to record in a set period. Utilization is the share of your available time that turns into billable work. If you keep missing the number, the cause is often your tracking, your calendar or your write-ups, not only your effort. This guide covers the cost, the causes and fixes you can use on a Mac today.
tldr: A billable hour target is a number your firm sets. Utilization is the share of your available time that gets billed.
Published surveys link billable pressure with mental health strain, so the cost is personal as well as financial.
Many gaps come from unrecorded time, admin work and slow write-ups, not from a lack of work.
Measure one month of real time before you change anything. A rough baseline beats a guess.
Lazur can explain what is on screen, point at fields, dictate logs, set reminders and draft notes. It does not track your time for you.

blocks.text: What a billable hour target actually measures

A billable hour target is a number your firm sets for a period. It might be weekly, monthly or annual. Utilization is a different number. It shows what share of your available time became billable work. Firms define both differently, so start by asking which hours count as available. Some firms count leave in that total. Some do not. Your percentage can look bad or good based on that one choice.

Read the two numbers together. Billable hours tell you how much you billed. Utilization tells you how much of your time went to billable work. A lawyer can log many hours and still have weak utilization if much of the week goes to unbilled work. Look at both before you decide whether you are behind.
What missing the target costs you

The first cost is usually personal, not financial. Long hours and constant billing pressure show up in health research on lawyers. A study by Krill and Anker, published in the Journal of Affective Disorders, reports nearly 48% of attorneys at high or very high burnout. The same study reports 21.7% with moderate to extremely severe depression symptoms. It also reports greater depression, stress and anxiety among lawyers with higher billable hours.

A 2025 survey by ALM and Law.com points the same way. It drew more than 3,100 lawyers and staff, mostly from large firms. Of those, 65.5% said billable-hour pressures hurt their mental well-being. That figure was nearly four points higher than the year before. Because the sample skews toward big firms, treat it as a signal, not a national count.

Hours are the other side of the cost. In a 2021 PLOS ONE study of 2,863 lawyers from the California Lawyers Association and the D.C. Bar, about 67% of women and men reported working over 40 hours in a typical week. Among women, 22.1% worked 51 or more hours. Among men, 27.1% did. Those samples are California and D.C. lawyers, so read them as a pattern, not a verdict on your firm.
Where the cost shows up in your week

items: Evenings and weekends used to catch up on time you did not log during the day.
Review conversations that focus on a short year, even when the cause was unlogged work.
Skipped breaks and lunches, so the daily number holds up on paper.
Rushed write-ups that take longer to fix later, or get cut before the invoice.
Strained trust with your team when the target feels impossible to reach.

blocks.title: Get your own numbers
blocks.text: The sources behind this guide do not put a dollar figure on a missed target. Ask your finance team for your firm's write-off and realization figures before you decide what matters most.
Why the target keeps slipping

Most targets slip for ordinary reasons. Time happens during the day and gets lost before it reaches the timesheet. Admin, email and internal meetings fill slots you thought were free. Then a matter runs longer than planned and the write-up lands late. Each cause is small. Together they open a gap that grows quietly across a month.

Before you blame yourself, check the mechanics. Pull your last month of time entries. Compare the total with the target. Then look at where the hours went. If the gap sits in unlogged time, the fix is in tracking. If it sits in admin, the fix is in your calendar. If it sits in write-offs, the fix is in scoping and billing terms.
How to measure the gap in one month

Start with a month, not a single week. One week can mislead you. A trial, a holiday or a long deposition can skew it. Export your entries from whatever tool you use. If you track time in your head or on paper, rebuild the month from calendar events and sent mail. The goal is an honest baseline, even a rough one.

items: Open Calendar and switch to Month view with ⌘3. List the client meetings, court dates and internal blocks.
Search your sent mail in Apple Mail for each client name. Use the search field at the top of the window.
Mark each block as billable, non-billable or unknown. The unknown pile tells you what you did not record.
Add the billable total and divide it by the hours you were available to bill. That is your utilization for the month.
Write the gap in one sentence and keep it in a note you can find again.

blocks.text: The math is simple once the inputs are clean. Take the target and subtract your billable total to get the gap. Divide billable hours by available hours to get utilization. If your available hours match your calendar, the denominator is clean. If they do not, write down what you excluded and why.
Tracking time on a Mac without losing the thread

Manual timers fail when you are deep in a document. You forget to start them, or you forget to stop them. Automatic tools watch the app and file the time to a matter for you. Timing is one Mac option. Its page says it captures time per file in Word, Keynote and Acrobat Pro, and while you browse for legal research. It also says entries sync back to Clio, with billing states of Not Billable, Billable, Billed and Paid.

Timing offers a 30-day free trial with no credit card required, according to its page. The page does not show a price, so check Timing's pricing before you commit. This guide did not verify Clio's current Mac features. Confirm the Clio sync with Clio directly before you rely on it.

No tracker fixes a target by itself. A tracker shows you the gap. It does not make you start earlier, cut low-value admin or scope a matter more tightly. Pick the tool that fits your habits, then change the habit that caused the gap.
Fixes you can use this week without buying anything

Start with the cheapest change. Block time for billable work before the day fills up. Put that block on your calendar as a named event, such as the matter you are working on. Other people will see it and plan around it. Keep admin in a separate, short block so it does not spread across the day.

Log time at the end of each matter, not at the end of the month. Memory fades within a day. A short line about the work is enough. Write the task, the matter and the time. If your entries live in mail, see [Outlook for lawyers on Mac](/for/lawyers/outlook) for ways to file and search them faster.

Write-offs deserve their own look. If a matter keeps losing time to the same task, scope it differently next time. Agree on the estimate and a check-in point with the partner before you start. Then flag any change in writing. That conversation is harder than logging time, but it moves the number more.

Ask your manager for the definition in writing. Which tasks count as billable? Do training, pro bono and business development count? What happens to time on a matter that closes early? A written answer ends most arguments before they start. The ABA passed a 2025 resolution on billable-hour credit for time off by 200 to 144. The article gives no data on whether such policies work, so use it as a starting point for a conversation.

blocks.title: Keep the agreed rule
blocks.text: Write down the target and the billable definition you agreed to. Store it next to your tracker, with the date, so you can check it when a question comes up.
Mistakes that make the numbers look worse than they are

items: Logging a whole week on Friday. Recall errors hide the real pattern.
Counting internal admin as billable because it felt like work for a client.
Ignoring the difference between time recorded and time billed. A tracker may show them as separate states.
Treating one bad week as a trend. Look at the full month before you panic.
Forgetting write-offs. Hours cut before the invoice still show where the time went.
Tracking everything and reviewing nothing. A log only helps when you read it each week.

blocks.text: Using AI tools with client work

AI tools can cut time on the admin side of this problem. You can use them to draft a status email or summarize a long thread. A randomized trial with law students at Minnesota and Michigan found AI tools raised productivity by 34% to 140%. Accuracy was mixed. The trial did not test your practice, so treat that range as a reason to run your own small test.

Client data needs care. Lazur listens and looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Even so, follow your employer's rules on client and matter data before you use any AI tool near privileged files. If your firm bans AI tools, the answer is no, whatever the product says.
A one-week routine to start

Use the routine below as a starting point, not a rule. Shift the timing to fit your day. The aim is to see the gap by the end of the week. You also want one protected block of billable work each day, and a log you review once.
When the target is the problem

Some targets are out of reach for the work you are given. If you have tracked a full month and the gap stays wide, the target may be the issue. Bring the data to your manager. Show the billable hours, the admin, and the write-offs. Ask what would have to change: staffing, matter mix, or the target itself.

Watch your own signals too. The research above links long hours with depression and stress in large samples. If you are sleeping badly, dreading work, or feeling low most days, talk to a doctor or your firm's wellbeing program. This page cannot assess that for you.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. It does not track your billable time. It does not click buttons, operate other apps or edit files for you. It helps with the friction around this problem. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask where a field sits on screen, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to do a task, and it guides you one click at a time.

Hold fn to dictate your end-of-day log at the cursor in any app. Ask Lazur to set a reminder, then have it draft a note to your manager about the target. Edit the draft yourself before you send it. Research jobs run in Lazur's own Chrome tabs and come back with a summary and a report, which helps when you gather public material on a firm policy. Check every source before you rely on it.
If the voice side fits your work, read the [pricing page](/pricing) or [download Lazur](/download). Check your firm's AI and client-data rules first.

faq.question: What is a good billable hour target for a lawyer?
faq.answer: The sources behind this guide do not give a benchmark number, so do not trust a figure you find without a source. Ask your firm for the target in writing, along with the definition behind it. If the target looks out of line with your practice area, bring your own data to your manager.

faq.question: What is the difference between billable hours and utilization?
faq.answer: Billable hours is the time you billed. Utilization is the share of your available time that went to billable work. A lawyer can bill many hours and still have weak utilization if much of the week goes to unbilled work. Check which measure your firm uses for targets.

faq.question: How do I calculate utilization on a Mac?
faq.answer: Add your billable hours for the period. Divide that total by the hours you were available to bill. Keep the result in a note, a spreadsheet or Numbers. Use the same definition of available time every month so the trend means something.

faq.question: Can an app track billable time automatically?
faq.answer: Some can. Timing says it captures time per file in Word, Keynote and Acrobat Pro, and while browsing for legal research. It offers a 30-day free trial with no credit card. Check the vendor's page for current pricing, and test any tool on a light week before you rely on it.

faq.question: Is Lazur a time tracker?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not track billable time. It can answer questions about what is on screen, point at fields, dictate text, set reminders and draft messages. It does not click buttons or edit files for you.

faq.question: Can I use AI tools with client files?
faq.answer: Follow your employer's rules on client and matter data first. If your firm restricts AI tools, do not use them with those files. Lazur listens and looks only while you hold the shortcut, and it says audio and screenshots are not stored.

faq.question: Does a billable target affect my pay or reviews?
faq.answer: The sources here do not say how any firm uses targets in pay or reviews. Ask your firm how billable numbers feed into reviews and bonuses. Get the answer in writing if you can.

faq.question: What should I do if the workload feels unsafe?
faq.answer: Talk to a doctor if you feel low, cannot sleep, or dread work most days. This guide cannot assess your health. Ask your firm whether it has a confidential support or wellbeing program, and how to reach it.

costs.title: Your evenings and weekends
costs.text: When the number is short, the gap often gets worked off after hours. That time is real, but it rarely shows up in the log. You work more and still see the same gap on the report. That loop feeds burnout.

costs.title: Your health and mood
costs.text: Published research links billable pressure with mental health strain. One study reports nearly 48% of attorneys at high or very high burnout, and 21.7% with moderate or worse depression symptoms. These are population figures, not a diagnosis, but they deserve attention.

costs.title: Your review and your bonus
costs.text: Some firms weigh billable numbers in reviews. A short year can change the tone of a conversation, even when the cause was unlogged work. Without a record, you cannot easily show what you did. The log matters as much as the work.

costs.title: Your team's workload and trust
costs.text: When a target seems impossible, colleagues often cover for each other, and hand-offs get messy. Work a partner expects by a certain date can slip. Clear numbers help everyone plan the week and the matter load.

costs.title: Client invoices and trust
costs.text: Late bills and write-offs often come from a gap between the work done and the work recorded. Invoices that seem unexplained make clients ask questions. Better logs help you explain the work and keep the relationship steady.

causes.title: Time never reaches the log
causes.text: Work happens across many apps, and the log lives somewhere else. A call that runs long, a document you reread, or an email answered on your phone often goes unrecorded. By Friday the day is a blur. You bill less because you cannot prove the work, not because the work did not happen.

causes.title: Admin fills the calendar
causes.text: Internal meetings, expense reports, conflict checks and training take real hours. They rarely bill. When they land between client slots, the billable count drops. You may feel busy and still see low utilization on the report.

causes.title: Matters run longer than planned
causes.text: A matter scoped at one estimate often grows when discovery or a counterparty change arrives. The clock keeps running, but the client may not pay for every hour. Write-offs follow, and they cut into the billed total.

causes.title: Late write-ups and slow entries
causes.text: Time spent drafting only counts if it gets entered. A draft finished on Tuesday but logged the next Monday loses detail. Late entries often lose context, which makes them easier to cut.

causes.title: Unclear rules about what counts
causes.text: If your firm has not defined billable work in writing, each lawyer guesses. Training, pro bono and business development may count in one group and not in another. Two people can do similar work and report different utilization. A written rule ends most of that confusion.

causes.title: Pressure that pushes time off the record
causes.text: When the target feels out of reach, some lawyers skip breaks or keep working after they log out. The data then understates effort and makes the picture look better than the reality. The target can look fine to managers and impossible to you.

fixes.title: Protect a daily billable block
fixes.text: Put one long block of billable work on your calendar each day. Name it after the matter you are working on. Decline new internal meetings that land inside it. In Apple Calendar, use File > New Event or press ⌘N.

fixes.title: Log each matter before you leave it
fixes.text: Write one line per matter before you move on. Include the task, the matter and the time. A short line written the same day beats a detailed one written next week. Pair it with a daily reminder in Apple Reminders.

fixes.title: Batch the admin
fixes.text: Group expense reports, conflict checks and internal email into one short block. Protect the rest of the day for client work. Batching keeps admin from scattering across every hour and every task switch.

fixes.title: Get the billable definition in writing
fixes.text: Ask for a short written rule on what counts as billable, non-billable and write-off time. Keep the answer in a note with the date. Refer to it when a question comes up, and ask again if the rule changes.

fixes.title: Scope matters before you start
fixes.text: Agree on an estimate and a check-in point with the partner before work begins. If the work runs past it, flag the change in writing. Scoping protects the number before any time is spent on the matter.

fixes.title: Try an automatic tracker if manual logs keep failing
fixes.text: If you forget to log, a tracker that captures activity can help. Timing says it captures time per file in Word and while browsing for research. Try the free trial on a light week, compare the captured time with your calendar, then decide.

fixes.title: Review the log once a week
fixes.text: Spend a short block on Friday reading the log. Look for unlogged gaps and recurring admin. Adjust next week's block based on what you see, and keep the change small enough to stick.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Measure the gap
plan.text: Pull the last month of entries from your tracker, calendar and sent mail. Mark each block billable, non-billable or unknown. Write the gap in one sentence and keep it in a note you can find again.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Ask for the rule
plan.text: Email your manager for the written definition of billable, non-billable and write-off time. Use Lazur to draft the note if that helps, then edit it and send it yourself.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Block billable time
plan.text: Create one daily block for the matter you work on most. Name it, add it to your calendar, and decline internal meetings that land inside it. Keep admin in its own short block.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Log as you go
plan.text: Log each matter before you leave it. Set a daily reminder in Apple Reminders for late afternoon. Dictate the log with fn if typing slows you down.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Review the week
plan.text: Read the week's entries next to your blocks. Note recurring admin and unlogged gaps. Choose one change for next week and write it down before you close the note.
